item.title: Limbic network hyperconnectivity, fasting appetite hormone dysregulation and impaired go/no-go performance in youths with bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BJPsych open
Bipolar disorder in youths is associated with metabolic dysregulation, impaired inhibitory control and limbic network connectivity changes. To investigate whether limbic network connectivity is associated with appetite hormones and inhibitory control in youths with bipolar disorder. The current study included 68 youths with bipolar disorder and 57 age- and gender-matched controls. They completed clinical assessments, the go/no-go (GNG) task, fasting appetite hormone (leptin, adiponectin, insulin and ghrelin) tests and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Region of interest (ROI)-to-ROI functional connectivity was analysed across 17 limbic ROIs. Cluster-level inferences were derived by using threshold-free cluster enhancement with family-wise error correction (p < 0.05). Furthermore, associations with appetite hormones and GNG task parameters were investigated. Compared with the control individuals, youths with bipolar disorder exhibited elevated leptin (p = 0.005) and insulin levels (p < 0.001), poorer performance on the GNG task and hyperconnectivity within the limbic network, identifying a significant cluster comprising the right anterior parahippocampal gyrus (aPHG)-right thalamus and right aPHG-hypothalamus edges (cluster-level family-wise error-corrected p = 0.045). No significant correlations were observed between limbic hyperconnectivity, appetite hormone levels and GNG task performance. Current cross-sectional cohort indicates that youths with bipolar disorder exhibit concurrent alterations in appetite hormones, inhibitory control and limbic connectivity. These findings provide a characterisation of youth bipolar disorder across multiple indices, although longitudinal studies are necessary to understand how these features relate to long-term clinical trajectories.

item.title: Associations between nonfatal strangulation-related brain injury in intimate partner violence and resting-state functional connectivity.
item.description:
Neuropsychology
Examine the association between nonfatal strangulation-related probable brain injury (NFS-BI), resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC), and verbal memory, among females who experienced physical intimate partner violence (IPV). Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging was analyzed for 110 females aged 18-60 years who experienced physical IPV. rsFC was characterized by seven graph theory metrics across three brain parcellation atlases (Power, Seitzman, and Schaefer-456 Parcellation[4S]). Responses to the Brain Injury Screening Questionnaire determined IPV-head trauma frequency, experience of probable NFS-BI, and other/additional non-IPV and IPV-related BI. Verbal memory was characterized by three measures from the California Verbal Learning Test, Third Edition: (a) Long Delay, Free Recall, (b) Trials 1-5 correct index scores, and (c) memory retention from Trials 1-5 to Long Delay, Free Recall. NFS-BI was significantly associated with reductions in within-default mode network (DMN) connectivity (Power: B = -0.03, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -0.03, p = .005; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .03), DMN segregation (Power: B = -0.04, p = .006; Seitzman: B = -0.04, p = .007; 4S: B = -0.03, p = .02), and global modularity (Power: B = -0.01, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -0.02, p = .008; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .007). Interactions between NFS-BI and within-DMN strength (Power: B = -150.05, p = .03; Seitzman: B = -212.11 p = .01; 4S: B = -204.52, p = .002), DMN segregation (Power: B = -106.97, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -114.54 p = .008; 4S: B = -189.88, p < .001), and modularity (Power: B = -373.80, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -367.35, p = .001; 4S: B = -312.55, p = .006) were significantly associated with memory retention. Those who experienced probable NFS-BI demonstrated altered rsFC compared with those who did not. Interactions between DMN rsFC and NFS-BI were significantly associated with memory retention. Future work should assess individuals with NFS-BI longitudinally to understand its effects on long-term brain health. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

item.title: State-independent functional connectomic architecture captures transdiagnostic network alterations and clinical variation
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Psychiatric disorders show substantial overlap across diagnostic categories while differing markedly in clinical expression. Whether these shared abnormalities and individual differences are embedded in stable functional brain architecture rather than in state-specific connectivity remains unclear. Methods: We integrated functional connectomes across one resting-state and six task-based fMRI conditions in 377 participants from the YaleNeuroConnect cohort, including 223 healthy controls and 154 individuals with psychiatric disorders. Principal component analysis was applied to each participant's functional connectivity data across the seven states to derive a state-independent connectivity representation. Network-based statistics then identified components showing significant case-control differences. Cross-state consistency was assessed, and findings were validated in an independent UCLA cohort of 177 participants. Associations between component expression and clinical measures were further examined within the Yale psychiatric group. Results: Cross-paradigm connectivity revealed two reproducible patterns of state-independent network alteration. One pattern showed reduced connectivity among limbic, somatomotor and salience systems, whereas the other showed stronger cerebellar coupling with limbic and somatomotor systems. Both patterns showed consistent case-control differences across functional states and generalized to an independent UCLA cohort. Their clinical relevance, however, differed. Greater expression of the cerebello-cortical connectivity pattern was associated with lower positive affect, greater psychopathology and more everyday executive difficulties, whereas the reduced limbic-somatomotor-salience connectivity pattern showed no significant clinical associations. Conclusions: These findings delineate a stable reorganization of large-scale functional architecture across psychiatric disorders and suggest that broadly expressed psychiatric abnormalities and individual clinical variation may be differentially represented within the altered connectome.

item.title: Frontoparietal functional connectivity underlies top-down attention in mild cognitive impairment
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment frequently show attention problems such as reduced top-down control, the ability to ignore task-irrelevant information. It is unclear whether this reduction corresponds with decreased brain connectivity. We aimed to determine whether and how differences in functional connectivity, or the correlated activity between brain areas, explain differences in top-down control in amnestic mild cognitive impairment. We conducted a case-control study with 26 patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (58-91 years; 10 women) and 29 age-matched healthy older adults (60-79 years; 9 women). All patients and control participants underwent neuropsychological assessment to confirm diagnosis and healthy cognitive status, respectively. We used resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging at 3T to analyse functional connectivity. Top-down control was estimated with a 'theory of visual attention'-based verbal partial-report task (parameter α ; higher α indicates poorer control). We identified visual and attention-relevant functional brain networks and tested for differences between patients and controls while controlling for age and gender. Compared with healthy control participants, patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment showed lower functional connectivity in the left frontoparietal attention network and in one visual network and worse top-down control α (t(37.43) = -2.24, p = 0.031). The reduced connectivity in the frontoparietal network, but not the visual network, significantly correlated with top-down control α across all participants (ρ = -0.33, p = 0.003) and in the patient group (ρ = -0.48, p = 0.014). Moreover, connectivity in the frontoparietal network mediated the relationship between amnestic mild cognitive impairment and top-down control α. These results link lower frontoparietal connectivity to worse attentional control in patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment. Worse control reflects inefficient attentional selection and increasing distraction by irrelevant information during perceptual processing and encoding into working memory. Overall, this implicates a role for the frontoparietal network in maintaining cognitive control or, more generally, supporting cognitive functioning in older adults with emerging cognitive impairment.

item.title: Resting-State EEG Theta-Band Functional Connectivity Characterizes Heterogeneity in Internet Gaming Disorder
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background. Symptom-based assessments capture IGD severity but provide limited information about neurophysiological heterogeneity. We examined whether resting-state EEG amplitude envelope correlation (AEC) profiles relate to IGD symptoms and reveal connectivity-defined heterogeneity. Methods. Thirty participants with IGD and thirty healthy controls underwent five-minute eyes-closed resting-state EEG. Source-level AEC was estimated across theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Exploratory representational similarity analysis tested associations between connectivity-profile dissimilarity and IGD-20 differences; theta-AEC profiles within IGD were further examined using principal component analysis and k-means clustering. Results. Within IGD, theta-AEC dissimilarity was associated with mood-modification differences ( rₛ = 0.277, p FDR = 0.020), whereas the corresponding association in controls was not significant. Exploratory clustering indicated connectivity heterogeneity, with the largest difference involving Visual–Salience/Ventral Attention connectivity; clusters did not differ in IGD-20 scores or weekly gaming time. Conclusions. Theta-AEC may capture symptom-related neurophysiological variation within IGD.

item.title: Functional Connectivity Gradients Reveal Cortical Hierarchical Reorganization Across the Cirrhosis–Hepatic Encephalopathy Spectrum
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a common neurocognitive complication of cirrhosis, but how macroscale cortical hierarchy is reorganized across the cirrhosis–HE spectrum remains incompletely understood. We characterized functional connectome gradient alterations across clinically defined cirrhosis stages and examined their clinical correlates. Methods This cross-sectional study included 104 participants: 35 patients with HE, 33 with cirrhosis without HE (NHE), and 36 healthy controls. Resting-state functional MRI was used to derive the first three connectivity gradients (G1–G3). Group differences were assessed at global, network, and cortical-parcel levels, and associations with blood ammonia, liver disease severity, and cognition were examined in patients with cirrhosis. Results Both NHE and HE showed reduced G1 range and variance versus healthy controls, indicating compression of the sensorimotor-to-transmodal hierarchy. Both groups showed higher somatomotor G1 and lower control and default mode G1, whereas HE additionally showed lower limbic G1. The only significant HE–NHE parcel-level difference involved the right temporal pole. Higher ammonia was associated with higher somatomotor G1 and lower control and default mode G1, while greater liver disease severity was associated mainly with lower limbic and default mode G1. Poorer cognition showed broadly corresponding associations. G2 and G3 did not differ among groups, and the main findings remained robust in sensitivity analyses. Conclusion NHE and HE showed largely shared compression of the sensorimotor-to-transmodal hierarchy, with more selective HE-associated alterations, particularly in temporolimbic regions. These abnormalities were associated with ammonia burden, liver disease severity, and cognitive impairment, supporting altered cortical functional hierarchy as a clinically relevant systems-level phenotype across the cirrhosis–HE spectrum.

item.title: Eyes-open resting-state EEG microstate analysis using ratio-normalized parameters across four- and seven-class solutions in healthy controls, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundResting-state EEG microstate analysis indexes large-scale network dynamics, yet the value of ratio-normalized temporal parameters under the eyes-open resting (EOR) condition remains unexplored across the cognitive decline continuum.ObjectiveTo examine whether ratio-normalized microstate parameters from four- and seven-class clustering solutions under EOR differentiate healthy controls (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD).MethodsOne hundred and eighty participants (HC, MCI, and AD; n = 60 each) were recruited from a hospital-based cohort in an elderly Korean population. Resting-state EEG recorded under EOR was analyzed using MICROSTATELAB in EEGLAB. Absolute temporal parameters (duration, occurrence, coverage) and ratio-normalized forms (relative duration, relative occurrence) were compared using ANCOVA with age as covariate, false discovery rate (FDR) correction, and Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons.ResultsIn the four-class solution, three parameters reached nominal significance, none surviving FDR correction across the full set of 20 tests: coverage of Microstate B (visual network; F(2176) = 3.561, p = 0.030), relative occurrence of Microstate B (F(2176) = 5.281, p = 0.006), and relative occurrence of Microstate E (executive network; F(2176) = 3.816, p = 0.024). MCI showed higher visual and lower executive microstate engagement than AD (p ≤ 0.023); no contrast involving HC was significant. Absolute occurrence parameters were non-significant whereas their ratio-normalized counterparts were significant. The seven-class solution yielded no corrected effects.ConclusionsRatio-normalized EOR microstate parameters distinguished MCI from AD through visual and executive network engagement, with small-to-moderate effects and HC intermediate. The four-class solution outperformed the seven-class solution, contrasting with eyes-closed reports. As these analyses were exploratory and did not survive correction, confirmation in independent cohorts is required.

item.title: Slow Oscillations Modulate Overnight Brain Changes in Working Memory Function.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Working memory (WM), the transient storage and manipulation of information, is a cognitive function that can improve with training. Accumulating evidence suggests that sleep, particularly slow oscillations (SOs) that occur during nonrapid eye movement sleep, supports this improvement. Yet, how sleep and SOs in particular relate to neural processes supporting WM remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how WM-related neural activity evolves across nocturnal sleep and how these changes relate to neural processing during SOs. Participants performed a WM task during fMRI before and after sleep, with simultaneous EEG-fMRI capturing neural activity during the first 2.5 hr of sleep. Our results showed significant overnight changes in WM-related activity, characterized by reduced recruitment of the dorsal precuneus during WM encoding/maintenance phases and frontal regions during the retrieval phase of WM. In addition, sleep increased item-specific reinstatement in a sensory processing region during WM. This pattern of results suggests a combined influence of sleep on enhancing sensory reinstatement while reducing potential top-down control (i.e., reduced parietal and frontal activity). Critically, SO-related activity was directly linked to overnight activity changes: Stronger SO activation in the premotor cortex and ventromedial pFC predicted greater overnight reductions in WM-related activity, and multivoxel analyses in the ventral attention network revealed a parallel relationship. These findings suggest that SOs play a critical role in WM function by facilitating the reorganization of WM-related processing.

item.title: Resting-State and Task-State Dual-Paradigm fNIRS Study Reveals Dynamic Alterations in Brain Network Activity in Alzheimer's Disease With Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms.
item.description:
Psychogeriatrics : the official journal of the Japanese Psychogeriatric Society
Background Alzheimer's disease (AD) frequently presents with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), severely impacting prognosis. The dynamic brain network mechanisms remain unclear, and traditional neuroimaging faces limitations. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers a unique approach to explore these mechanisms under natural conditions. Objective To systematically compare brain region activation, signal complexity and network topology in AD patients with and without BPSD using resting-state and verbal fluency task (VFT) fNIRS paradigms. Methods This cross-sectional study enrolled 48 AD patients (24 with BPSD, 24 without) and 25 normal controls (NC). fNIRS recorded hemodynamic changes in the frontal, temporal, parietal and occipital lobes during rest and VFT. Analyses included activation, time-frequency characteristics, functional connectivity and network topology. Partial correlations assessed links between fNIRS metrics and neuropsychological scores. Results In resting state, AD-BPSD showed altered coefficient of variation in left premotor and somatosensory cortices, and elevated information entropy in left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (lDLPFC), versus NC and AD-non-BPSD. Functional connectivity abnormalities emerged between right frontal eye field-left somatosensory cortex, and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC)-left superior temporal gyrus (lSTG) (p < 0.05). During VFT, AD-BPSD had significantly lower lDLPFC and left somatosensory activation versus NC (p < 0.05), but increased signal fluctuation and power in right primary motor cortex (rM1) (p < 0.05), alongside reduced whole-brain clustering coefficient (p = 0.023). Conclusions AD-BPSD was associated with altered brain functional patterns across resting and task states, involving sensorimotor and executive networks as well as altered interhemispheric coordination. These fNIRS-derived alterations provide exploratory evidence of altered brain functional patterns associated with BPSD and warrant further investigation in larger longitudinal studies.

item.title: Nucleus Accumbens and Ventral Tegmental Area Functional Connectivity as a Marker of Reward Sensitivity in Infancy.
item.description:
Developmental science
Early functional connectivity within the brain's reward circuitry may provide insight into the developmental origins of individual differences in pleasure and motivation. This study examined resting-state functional connectivity between two key reward-related regions, the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and ventral tegmental area (VTA), in 94 one-month-old infants (58% male; M = 4.84 weeks, SD = 0.86) and its association with later reward-related temperament. Infants completed a resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging scan during natural sleep with a mean of 11.09 (SD = 2.78) min of retained low-motion data. Caregivers reported their infants' temperament at age six months, including high- and low-intensity pleasure as indicators of individual differences relevant to reward sensitivity. Positive resting-state functional connectivity between the NAc and VTA was present in early infancy (Cohen's d = 0.44, 95% CI [0.22, 0.65]), p < 0.001). Less positive NAc-VTA connectivity was associated with greater high-intensity pleasure at six months (β = -0.32, 95% CI [-0.54, -0.10], p = 0.004), indicating that infants with stronger connectivity between these regions exhibited less enjoyment of highly stimulating, energetic activities. NAc-VTA connectivity was not associated with low-intensity pleasure (β = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.24, 0.21], p = 0.908). These findings suggest that early variation in mesolimbic connectivity may serve as a marker of emerging individual differences in reward responsiveness, with implications for understanding affective development in infancy.

item.title: Altered brain-state dynamics and associations with dependence severity and affective-somatic burden in cocaine use disorder.
item.description:
Addictive behaviors
Cocaine use disorder (CUD) is characterized not only by impaired cognitive control but also by pronounced emotion dysregulation. Although resting-state brain dynamics have been linked to adaptive cognitive and emotional functioning, it remains unclear how these dynamics are altered in CUD and whether such alterations relate to dependence severity and affective-somatic symptom burden. We applied Hidden Markov modeling to resting-state fMRI from 58 individuals with CUD and 44 healthy controls to characterize large-scale brain-state dynamics. CUD was associated with reduced global switching, increased occupancy and persistence of a limbic-dominant state, reduced occupancy of a frontoparietal-ventral attention state, and prolonged persistence of a ventral attention-somatomotor state. Transition analyses further identified higher transition probabilities from default mode-dorsal attention and ventral attention-somatomotor configurations toward the limbic-dominant state. Limbic-state occupancy showed positive associations with dependence severity, emotion dysregulation, somatization, and anxiety. Meta-analytic decoding provided functional context for this state, while exploratory spatial comparisons with normative receptor and gene-expression atlases provided molecular context. Together, these findings identify altered resting-state temporal organization in CUD and suggest that limbic-state occupancy is a potential correlate of dependence severity and affective-somatic burden.

item.title: SPARK-ICA: Guided Frequency-Resolved Dynamic Spatial ICA Reveals Fine-Scale fMRI Network Dynamics.
item.description:
Human brain mapping
Fine-scale spatiotemporal dynamics of functional brain networks are increasingly recognized as critical markers of transient connectivity and neuropsychiatric pathology. However, many existing dynamic fMRI methods primarily focus on temporal variability without explicitly resolving the spatial-frequency content of network dynamics, potentially limiting characterization of subtle, high-frequency spatial reconfigurations. To address this gap, we propose SPARK-ICA (Spatial-frequency Partitioned, Adaptive Reconstruction using Knowledge-guided ICA), a frequency-resolved dynamic spatial independent component analysis (ICA) framework that integrates NeuroMark template guidance with spatial frequency decomposition and group-level ICA of time-resolved, band-specific spatial maps. Starting from template-guided NeuroMark networks, we first estimate time-varying spatial maps using a dynamic guided ICA approach, capturing subject-specific network expression over time. Each dynamic spatial map is then decomposed into multiple spatial frequency bands using Fourier-domain spatial filtering, isolating fine- to coarse-scale spatial features at each time point. Band-specific spatial maps are subsequently concatenated and subjected to a blind group-level multi-frequency ICA, yielding a compact latent representation in which each dynamic component is characterized by distinct spatial-frequency signatures. These group-level band-resolved components are then used as references to estimate subject- and band-specific time courses and maps via spatially constrained ICA, enabling frequency-specific analysis of both long-term correlations and short-term temporal variability while preserving reproducibility across subjects. Using resting-state fMRI data from schizophrenia (SZ) patients and healthy controls (HC), we evaluated both long-term correlations and short-term variability of band-resolved dynamic time courses. For the group-level analyses, we focused on a predefined subset of NeuroMark networks with well-established involvement in SZ-related dysconnectivity. Our results reveal frequency-specific abnormalities in SZ, with enhanced long-term connectivity within sensory and subcortical networks and pronounced short-term alterations involving predominantly higher-frequency spatial components, particularly in cerebellar and subcortical systems. These findings indicate that SZ-related dysregulation is differentially expressed across spatial-frequency and temporal scales, rather than reflecting uniform dysconnectivity. Together, this framework provides a unified approach for analyzing dynamic fMRI networks across spatial, temporal, and frequency dimensions, extending our previous NeuroMark-DyFICA framework from a predominantly high-frequency spatial representation to an explicitly frequency-resolved characterization of dynamic network organization. By explicitly modeling spatial frequency-dependent dynamics, the proposed method provides a more resolved characterization of network alterations and offers a framework for identifying candidate markers of neuropsychiatric disorders.

item.title: Functional Network Organization Underlying Individual Differences in False Feedback Susceptibility: A Graph Theoretical Analysis.
item.description:
Human brain mapping
Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false physiological feedback reflect variations in interoceptive processing, yet the underlying neural network mechanisms remain unclear. We analyzed resting-state functional connectivity using graph theoretical approaches in 41 healthy adults who completed a somatosensory false feedback paradigm. Nine regions of interest were defined from previous activation analyses, and network topology metrics including local efficiency, clustering coefficient, centrality measures, and path length were calculated across multiple thresholds. Three distinct patterns of network organization predicted false feedback susceptibility. Individuals more susceptible to false feedback showed: (1) increased posterior insula eccentricity, indicating network peripheralization of this key interoceptive region; (2) consistent orbitofrontal cortex segregation across multiple metrics including increased path length and decreased centrality measures; and (3) cerebellar network reconfiguration with reduced local efficiency but increased betweenness centrality. Somatosensory false feedback susceptibility reflects specific alterations in functional network topology, particularly reduced integration of interoceptive regions (posterior insula) and emotional appraisal systems (orbitofrontal cortex). These findings support a network-based model where interoceptive processing depends on efficient integration between visceral sensation, emotional evaluation, and cognitive control systems. Understanding these network properties may inform interventions targeting interoceptive awareness and emotional regulation.

item.title: Intrinsic Activity Reductions and Cerebello-Cortical Diaschisis-Like Mechanism in Friedreich Ataxia: An fALFF Resting-State fMRI Study.
item.description:
Brain and behavior
Background Friedreich ataxia (FA) is characterized by progressive degeneration of the cerebellum and its output pathways, particularly the dentato-thalamo-cortical system, leading to motor impairment and the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome (CCAS). Resting-state fMRI studies in FA have focused on alterations of long-range functional connectivity, but little is known about how intrinsic regional neural activity is affected within cerebello-cortical networks. Methods Twenty-eight adults with genetically confirmed FA and 28 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent resting-state functional MRI. Intrinsic brain activity was quantified using the fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF). Whole-brain comparisons were performed between controls and patients, and between patients with definite CCAS (FA-Cog) and cognitively preserved patients (FA-NoCog). Within the FA group, voxelwise regressions assessed associations between fALFF, motor severity (Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia [SARA]), and cognitive performance (Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome Scale [CCAS-S]), adjusting for age, sex, head motion, and cerebellar gray matter volume. Results Compared with controls, patients exhibited reduced fALFF in medial and lateral prefrontal regions. Higher SARA scores were associated with lower fALFF in occipital, sensorimotor, posterior cingulate, and cerebellar regions, whereas higher CCAS-S scores correlated with higher fALFF in bilateral prefrontal and cerebellar cognitive networks. Compared with FA-NoCog, FA-Cog patients showed lower fALFF in bilateral frontal and insular regions. Conclusions Resting-state fALFF reveals downstream dysfunction of distributed cerebello-cortical networks in FA. Associations with motor severity and cognition, together with additional fronto-insular dysfunction in patients with definite CCAS, support progressive cerebello-cortical disconnection consistent with a diaschisis-like mechanism.

item.title: Cortical traveling wave analysis reveals weaker resting forward theta waves and greater task-related modulation in obsessive compulsive disorder.
item.description:
Psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
Aims Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is associated with abnormalities in large-scale brain network dynamics. Conventional electroencephalography (EEG) captures local oscillatory activity but does not characterize spatiotemporal propagation patterns. This study investigates cortical traveling waves, which index directional information flow across the cortex, to determine whether they provide novel insights into altered neural communication in OCD. Methods Resting-state (eyes-closed) and task-based (Go/NoGo, Flanker) EEG were recorded from 25 individuals with OCD and 27 healthy controls (HCs). Traveling waves were quantified along midline electrodes using two-dimensional Fast Fourier Transforms to extract forward (posterior-to-anterior) and backward (anterior-to-posterior) propagation in theta (4-8Hz) and alpha (8-13Hz) bands. Group differences were assessed using Bayesian and frequentist linear mixed-effects models controlling for age and sex. Results At rest, a significant group-by-direction interaction was observed in the theta band (P = 0.0006), driven by weaker forward traveling wave strength in OCD relative to HC. No group differences were observed for backward waves or in the alpha band. During the Flanker task, the OCD group showed a significantly greater increase in forward theta wave strength from rest than HC (P = 0.022). No associations were found between traveling wave measures and symptom severity. Conclusion OCD is characterized by altered theta-band traveling wave dynamics, specifically reduced forward (bottom-up) signaling at rest, and increased task-related modulation during the Flanker task. These findings suggest disrupted hierarchical cortical communication and inefficient engagement of sensory-driven processes. The absence of symptom correlations suggests a potential trait-like neurophysiological marker or endophenotype of OCD.

item.title: Altered sensorimotor-occipital network topology in chronic insomnia: A graph-theoretical and edge-wise resting-state fMRI analysis.
item.description:
NeuroImage. Clinical
Objective The multi-level network aberrations in chronic insomnia (CI) and their neurobiological underpinnings remain elusive. Here, we applied graph-theoretical, edge-wise, and modular analyses to resting-state fMRI data to characterize systems-level functional network reorganization in CI patients. Methods Resting-state fMRI was acquired from CI patients and healthy controls (HCs). Whole-brain functional networks were parcellated using the Dosenbach-160 atlas, and then graph-theoretical, edge-wise, and modular analyses were performed. Group differences in global, nodal, edge-wise, and modular metrics were examined via a general linear model, with age, sex, education, and framewise displacement as covariates. Global and nodal metrics were corrected using the Bonferroni method; edge-wise comparisons used network-based statistics (NBS; cluster-forming threshold p < 0.001, 5000 permutations, FWE-corrected p < 0.05). Results Compared with HCs, CI patients showed significantly decreased average clustering coefficients, shorter path lengths, and reduced local efficiency, but increased global efficiency - a pattern indicative of a shift toward random network topology. Notably, normalized small-worldness scalar remained intact. Nodal clustering decreased in the left posterior occipital cortex. Edge-wise analysis revealed widespread connectivity disruptions involving parietal-posterior occipital, posterior insular-occipital, and dorsolateral prefrontal-temporal pathways. Modular analyses further demonstrated reduced connectivity both between sensorimotor and occipital networks, and within the sensorimotor network itself. Conclusions CI entails multi-level functional network reorganization, characterized by global topological randomization, reduced occipital nodal clustering, and selective decoupling within sensorimotor and sensorimotor-occipital circuits. These findings suggest that CI involves widespread integration failure across large-scale systems rather than isolated regional dysfunction, with potential implications for understanding its neurocognitive sequelae.

item.title: Age-related patterns in local spontaneous activity measured by fNIRS: greater unpredictability in infancy, local reorganization in childhood.
item.description:
Brain research bulletin
The maturation of the brain is typically described at the whole-brain scale, whereas age-related changes in spontaneous activity within local brain regions have received comparatively little attention. Resting-state regional dynamics (RSRD) are defined as the temporal variability characteristics of activity within a single brain region under the resting state, and can stably reflect the intrinsic properties of spontaneous brain activity. The present study compared two age periods: infants (1-8 months of age) recorded during natural sleep and children (4-15 years of age) recorded during wakeful rest, corresponding to distinct developmental stages of rapid postnatal structural and functional brain development. The results suggested markedly different age-related feature patterns between the two groups: during infancy the predominant change was an increase in unpredictability, with RSRD activity becoming increasingly complex, whereas during childhood the dominant feature was a systematic reorganization of local waveform patterns. Age-related RSRD changes in the prefrontal cortex suggested a linear trend in infancy and a mixed linear-nonlinear trend in childhood, with inter-regional differences in the magnitude of feature changes. Vascular maturation-related indices suggested an association with RSRD feature changes during infancy, but not during childhood, suggesting that vascular factors may play a relatively more prominent role in early developmental stages. External data and exploratory internal cross-validation provided preliminary support for the age-related nature of these features, although further validation in larger, independent cohorts is needed.

item.title: Full-Term and Preterm Differences in Human Brain Functional Connectivity Development Across Birth
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
We possess a limited understanding of how preterm and full-term brains develop during the earliest stages of life, from the fetal to neonatal period, and how they respond to the birth transition. Here, we characterize brain resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) using over 1000 longitudinal fetal and infant functional MRI scans from 21 to 52 post-conception weeks across birth. By mapping the developmental trajectory of RSFC across this window, we unveil marked divergences in developmental patterns between preterm- and term-born brains at both the global and network levels. When aligned by birth, the full-term group exhibit generally higher RSFC than the preterm group. For selected between-network connections with a significant prematurity effect, full-term cases demonstrate an overall increase in RSFC across age, whereas preterm cases show minimal change or even a decrease in connectivity of these systems. In contrast, when aligned by postconceptional age, the preterm group shows an accelerated increase in RSFC between 30 and 40 weeks. Across comparisons, mode of delivery and sex showed minimal influence on these trajectories. These findings offer novel insight into how prematurity and early exposure to the extrauterine environment alter the developmental trajectories of large-scale neural networks, advancing our understanding of both typical and preterm brain development.

item.title: Behavioral Markers of Essential Tremor Correlate with Distributed Alteration of Brain Functional Connectivity
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Essential Tremor (ET) is a common motor disorder characterized by involuntary oscillations of the upper limbs during voluntary movement. Although increasing evidence implicates dysfunction of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway, ET remains a diagnosis of exclusion, as no definitive biological marker currently exists. To better characterize ET, we recently hypothesized that impaired compensation of sensorimotor delays within the long-latency feedback pathways may generate the tremor-like oscillations observed in ET. This theory suggests that the mean spectral amplitude (MSA), derived from limb kinematics, may serve as a potential marker of ET. Here we investigated the relationship between MSA, standard clinical assessment (Fahn Tolosa Marin Tremor Rating Scale; FTM-TRS), and brain connectivity derived from resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). Using seed-based analyses, we replicated previous findings of reduced functional connectivity between the dentate nucleus and components of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway in ET patients compared with neurologically intact (NI) age-matched participants. Graph-theoretical analyses of whole-brain functional networks revealed distributed alterations in network topology across motor-related cortical and subcortical regions. Several graph metrics correlated with FTM-TRS scores and/or MSA, particularly within motor-related cortical and subcortical circuits, including the thalamus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum in ET. These findings indicate that ET is characterized by distributed alterations in functional brain networks beyond reduced connectivity of dentate nucleus and highlights MSA as a candidate quantitative marker linking altered brain connectivity to sensorimotor delay-driven tremor oscillations.

item.title: Pre-stress functional brain connectivity is associated with subsequent anxiety during war-related stress
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Individuals exposed to major real-world stressors show markedly different psychological outcomes, but whether this heterogeneity is associated with pre-existing neural characteristics remains unclear because neuroimaging is rarely performed beforehand. We acquired resting-state fMRI in healthy adults before the unforeseen onset of war-related stress. Approximately 13 months later, during ongoing war-related stress, participants (n = 31) were assessed for anxiety, depressive symptoms, perceived stress and post-traumatic stress symptoms. Among 144 associations spanning 36 predefined corticolimbic and reward-related connections and four outcomes, lower baseline functional connectivity between the right nucleus accumbens and right amygdala was associated with greater subsequent anxiety. This association survived permutation-based family-wise error correction and adjustment for baseline depressive symptoms, age and sex. These findings provide preliminary prospective evidence that pre-existing functional organization of threat- and reward-related circuitry is associated with individual differences in anxiety during prolonged adversity.

item.title: The effect of acupuncture-rehabilitation therapy on brain functional plasticity in motor aphasia after ischemic stroke: a randomized clinical neuroimaging trial.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Motor aphasia is the most prevalent type of aphasia following ischemic stroke (IS). This study aims to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and underlying neural mechanisms of acupuncture-rehabilitation (A-R) therapy on motor aphasia after IS. Twenty-six patients with post-IS motor aphasia were randomly assigned to either the A-R group or the Conventional Rehabilitation (CR) group in a 1:1 ratio, and matched by age and gender with 26 healthy controls (HCs). The CR group received standard treatment and language training, while the A-R group additionally underwent scalp acupoint cluster acupuncture. Behavioral assessments and Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (BOLD-fMRI) scans were conducted before and after the four-week intervention to evaluate therapeutic outcomes and underlying mechanisms. Compared to HCs, patients exhibited decreased Amplitude of Low Frequency Fluctuations (ALFF) in the right precuneus (p < 0.05) and reduced Regional Homogeneity (ReHo) in the left precuneus/postcentral gyrus (p < 0.05). Enhanced functional connectivity (FC) was observed in regions including the left Broca's area and right superior temporal gyrus, left Broca's area and right inferior frontal orbitalis gyrus, left Broca's area and right precentral gyrus, left Broca's area and right postcentral gyrus (p < 0.05). After intervention, significant improvements were observed in Aphasia Quotient (AQ) scores and sub-item performance in both patient groups (p < 0.05), with the A-R group showing greater gains in AQ and spontaneous speech scores compared to the CR group (p < 0.05). FMRI results indicated a significant increase in mean ALFF (mALFF) in the left inferior temporal gyrus after A-R treatment (p < 0.05) compared to before, and higher szReHo in the left anterior central gyrus compared to the CR group (p < 0.05). FC between the left Broca's area and right precentral gyrus decreased in the A-R group (p < 0.05). Additionally, a negative correlation was observed between the right anterior central gyrus and listening comprehension (r = -0.574, p = 0.020). The findings suggest that both A-R and CR therapies enhance language function in patients with motor aphasia post-IS, with A-R therapy demonstrating superior efficacy. The therapeutic mechanism of A-R likely involves activating left hemisphere brain regions, suppressing right hemisphere activity, and restoring hemispheric balance to facilitate functional recovery.

item.title: Naturalistic language assessment and brain-network biomarkers in post-stroke aphasia for precision neurorehabilitation

Frontiers in human neuroscience
