item.title: Affective representations and brain-body dynamics during emotional video viewing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Emotional events evoke changing neural and bodily responses, but how these responses relate to overall emotional evaluations and how brain and body responses correspond over time remain unclear. Ninety-two participants viewed 25 silent emotional videos, each approximately one minute long, and rated valence and arousal after each video. We recorded brain activity using magnetoencephalography alongside cardiac, electrodermal, respiratory and facial-muscle activity. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) compared source-resolved cortical spectral patterns and peripheral response patterns with participants' valence and arousal ratings, adjusting each affective dimension for the other. Across whole videos, valence similarity corresponded to beta-band power patterns predominantly in left sensorimotor and frontotemporal cortex and to facial-muscle responses. Arousal similarity corresponded to alpha-band power patterns in the right frontoparietal cortex and to phasic electrodermal activity. The neural associations persisted after adjustment for visual and semantic similarities between the videos. Windowed neural correspondence with retrospective valence was significant from around 10 s onwards, with both neural and facial-muscle associations strengthening towards the end of the videos, whereas no significant windowed arousal associations were detected throughout viewing. We further applied dynamic RSA to compare neural and physiological response patterns across videos at different temporal lags. Correspondence exceeded a temporally decoupled reference for facial muscles, heart rate and electrodermal activity, but not respiration rate. On average, corrugator activity preceded corresponding neural patterns by about 1 s, zygomaticus activity occurred at approximately the same time, and heart-rate and electrodermal activity followed about 1.7 s and 4.5 s later, respectively. Together, these findings link overall affective evaluations to complementary neural and peripheral response geometries and reveal signal-specific temporal profiles of ongoing brain-body correspondence.

item.title: A Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman Kernel Framework for Multimodal Brain Connectome Analysis
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract We introduce a Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman (WWL) graph-kernel framework for the joint analysis of weighted structural graphs and continuous node attributes, together with a regularized fractional-Laplacian extension of the underlying graph propagation operator. The proposed fractional operator provides non-local propagation across the entire graph, with influence decaying as a power law with graph distance, while remaining anchored to the subject-specific structural topology. This extends the standard finite-range Weisfeiler Lehman propagation scheme to a controlled long-range setting without introducing an externally prescribed coupling between structural and functional information. We formulate the framework for multimodal brain connectivity by representing each subject as a single attributed graph: diffusion tractography defines the weighted structural edges, while resting-state functional connectivity profiles are encoded as continuous node attributes. We evaluate the method on a synthetic cohort of $900$ subjects in three ordered clinical groups along the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, generated from multiple structural templates and characterised by a spatially structured loss of resting-state network segregation with age. Under nested cross-validation, the WWL kernel achieves a balanced accuracy of $0.651\pm0.028$, significantly outperforming both a raw-feature SVM and a histogram-based WL-kernel baseline. Controlled ablations separate the contribution of the Wasserstein representation from that of structural propagation. Replacing the propagation operator by the identity yields essentially identical classification performance, whereas a structure-only representation approaches chance, showing that the discriminative gain in this benchmark is primarily associated with the Wasserstein point-cloud representation rather than structural propagation. Conversely, experiments across distinct signal regimes show that the fractional extension is signal-dependent: non-local propagation can improve continuous prediction for diffuse whole-brain coupling signals, but provides no consistent advantage for network-segregation signals. We further identify a connectivity artefact induced by fixed-percentile structural sparsification and establish a threshold preserving graph connectivity across subjects. The results clarify the respective roles of Wasserstein geometry, structural propagation, and non-locality in multimodal graph representations and provide a controlled framework for assessing when fractional graph propagation is expected to be beneficial.

item.title: The dual future of OPM-MEG: Clinical translation and naturalistic neuroscience.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) has moved beyond proof of principle. The decisive question is no longer whether cryogen-free sensors can detect neuromagnetic fields from the human brain with sufficient sensitivity, but whether complete systems can deliver clinical decision value and interpretable recordings during more naturalistic behaviour. Here we argue that OPM-MEG is developing along two partly overlapping trajectories. One is clinical translation, where usefulness depends more on reliable workflows, calibrated source localisation, auditable quality control, and empirical evidence for improved diagnostic or treatment decisions. The other is naturalistic neuroscience, where wearable measurement can connect neural dynamics to movement, action, and social behaviour without conflating neural activity with movement-related artefacts. Both trajectories depend on a shared engineering stack including magnetic field control, dense spatial sampling, accurate calibration, integrated electronics, artefact suppression, participant comfort, and synchronised behavioural measurement. The next stage of OPM-MEG should be evaluated by clinical utility in specific patient groups, statistically identifiable neural dynamics in behaviourally rich settings, and sufficient system detail for replication across systems and sites.

item.title: Characteristic of anterior cingulate cortex connectivity at subregional level in major depressive disorder.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Background The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) exhibits substantial role underlying the pathophysiology of major depressive disorder (MDD), yet its exact connectivity alteration and the relationship with clinical symptoms remain unclarified. We aimed to systematically investigate ACC subregional functional connectivity alterations with a relatively large sample of MDD and their longitudinal changes associated with clinical state. Methods From the Huaxi Depression Imaging Cohort Study, we recruited 141 MDD patients and 138 matched healthy controls (HC) with complete clinical information and resting-state functional MRI data, and calculated functional connectivity (FC) of five ACC subregions (subgenual, perigenual, rostral, dorsal, and caudal ACC). A subset of patients who completed follow-up clinical assessments and MRI scanning was further classified into remitted and non-remitted subgroups. ACC subregional FC was compared between MDD and HC, and for longitudinal changes in remitted and non-remitted patients separately. Exploratory correlations between FC alterations and symptom profiles were also assessed. Results Compared with HCs, MDD patients demonstrated widespread hyperconnectivity between most ACC subregions and regions within frontoparietal network (FPN) and default mode network (DMN) at baseline. At follow-up, remitted patients showed reduced connectivity between perigenual ACC (pgACC) and dorsolateral/ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC/vlPFC), with connectivity approaching HC levels. Non-remitted patients, however, exhibited no significant changes. Conclusions Our findings delineate specific dysconnectivity patterns of ACC at the subregional level in MDD and suggest the pgACC-dlPFC/vlPFC connectivity may represent a candidate neuroimaging correlate of remission.

item.title: Altered stability of dynamic functional architecture in the co-occurrence of autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occur, whereas the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain largely unexplored. This study aimed to identify alterations in dynamic functional architecture across ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity. This study selected 287 participants from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange and ADHD-200 datasets, divided into ASD without ADHD (ASD-only), ADHD without ASD (ADHD-only), ASD + ADHD, and typically developing (TD) groups. In this study, we employed dynamic functional stability at the voxel level by measuring the temporal concordance of dynamic functional connectivity (DFC). Furthermore, whole-brain DFC analyses were conducted using clusters with significant stability alterations as seed regions. Group comparisons and correlation analyses were subsequently performed. Our results showed significant group differences in functional stability in the left superior frontal gyrus, orbital part (ORBsup), right pallidum, and left amygdala. Seed-based analyses identified altered DFC variability between the left amygdala and three regions, including the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG), the left insula, and the left superior occipital gyrus (SOG). Notably, DFC variability between the left amygdala and right MTG was significantly negatively correlated with Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ) scores in the comorbidity group (r = - 0.620, p < 0.01, FDR corrected). From a dynamic perspective, our findings revealed that ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity exhibited commonanduniquechanges in brain function, thereby enhancing our understanding of the pathogenesis underlying ASD + ADHD.

item.title: Altered centrality and connectivity in motor networks following Xingnao Kaiqiao acupuncture for acute ischemic stroke: a randomized controlled, exploratory fMRI study.
item.description:
Medical & biological engineering & computing
Xingnao Kaiqiao (XNKQ) acupuncture is recommended as an adjunctive intervention for motor dysfunction after acute ischemic stroke (AIS), yet its neuroplastic mechanisms remain unclear. In this randomized, exploratory study, 28 AIS patients were randomly assigned to XNKQ acupuncture plus medication (n = 14) or medication-only (n = 14) to receive 10 sessions of treatment over 14 days. Clinical assessments and resting-state fMRI scanning were conducted before and after the intervention, with brain reorganization analyzed using voxel-wise degree centrality (DC) and seed-based functional connectivity (FC). We found that better recovery in the XNKQ group, reflected by more improvements in NIHSS, total and upper-extremity FMA scores, was correlated with reduced DC in the ipsilesional primary motor cortex (iM1) concurrent with attenuated FC to the contralesional supplementary motor area (cSMA), alongside increased DC in the bilateral SMA and preserved FC between SMA and cerebellar regions. Further exploratory mediation analysis suggested that change in iM1-cSMA FC potentially mediated the relationship between iM1 DC normalization and motor recovery. These preliminary findings suggest that XNKQ acupuncture may facilitate early motor recovery after AIS through normalization of ipsilesional M1 hub centrality and modulation of M1-SMA cross-hemispheric connectivity, providing candidate network markers for acupuncture-associated neuroplasticity.

item.title: The interplay between cortical tracking and functional connectivity in musicians and non-musicians listening to speech and music
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Musical expertise is associated with auditory processing advantages which can extend to the speech domain. However, the origins of such domain-general benefits remain unclear. Recent frameworks propose that better rhythm processing in musicians might be at the basis of the observed advantages in processing music and speech. Auditory cortical tracking and inter-regional interactions between auditory and motor areas have been proposed as key neural mechanisms. In this study, we asked whether expertise-related increase in cortical tracking would be elicited by naturalistic stimuli in clear listening conditions, and whether such effects would be related to audiomotor functional connectivity and individual rhythmic abilities. We compared MEG data from expert musicians and controls with no musical playing experience while they listened to two-minutes long stories and excerpts of piano music. We also collected behavioral data in a rhythmic task testing speech (syllable) production. We found that musicians showed enhanced tracking and enhanced functional connectivity in both speech and music conditions, as well as better rhythmic abilities relative to non-musicians. Alpha connectivity between the right auditory cortex and inferior frontal gyrus negatively predicted cortical tracking across all participants in the speech condition, while no relation was observed for music. We suggest that stronger cortical tracking in musicians is due to domain-general differences in auditory sensory processes and is not driven by motor influences in our experiment. Moreover, a trade-off between cortical tracking and inter-regional communication might be at the basis of optimal perception of speech in both musicians and non-musicians in clear listening conditions.

item.title: Naturalistic Movie Viewing Reveals a Distributed Network Supporting Audiovisual Speech Processing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Traditional paradigms in cognitive neuroscience often fail to capture the richness of real-world experiences. To bridge this gap, researchers increasingly use naturalistic stimuli such as movies, which provide complex, multisensory input. Speech perception is a prime example of such complexity: it is inherently multisensory, involving the integration of auditory cues, lip movements, and facial expressions. Prior studies suggest that the left posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and superior temporal gyrus (STG) play a critical role in this integration. However, most studies of audiovisual speech have relied on simplified or artificial stimuli, limiting ecological validity. To address these gaps, we analyzed fMRI data from human participants watching two full-length films ( 500 Days of Summer, Citizenfour ) to assess the consistency of multisensory speech processes across distinct genres and narratives. We manually annotated word onset times and modality (audiovisual vs. auditory-only). Across two movies and 38 participants we observed consistent speech-related activation in the pSTS and STG across speech types. Compared to auditory-only speech, audiovisual speech recruited a broad left-lateralized network including the angular gyrus, posterior temporal cortex, temporal pole, and inferior frontal gyrus, along with the right cerebellum. These findings were also consistently present in single-subject data. Importantly, most of the regions observed in our analyses have been implicated in multisensory function in the nonhuman primate literature despite receiving relatively little focus in human neuroimaging. Together our results demonstrate that speech processing during naturalistic viewing recruits a distributed network extending substantially beyond regions traditionally emphasized in audiovisual speech research.

item.title: Brain Dynamics of Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness at Rest Reveal Alterations in Multisensory and Motor Areas
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness (PPPD) is a chronic functional disorder with unsteadiness and postural instability, attributed to altered multisensory integration and visual dependence. fMRI studies report altered connectivity in several regions, however, dynamic connectivity remains unexplored. Objectives We characterized resting-state brain dynamics in 17 patients with PPPD and 20 matched healthy controls (HC), and their relationship to clinical and postural measures. Methods Co-Activation Patterns (CAPs) were derived from resting-state fMRI scans for four seeds relevant to multisensory integration, motor output and vestibular processing – right temporo-parietal junction (rTPJ), caudate nucleus, hippocampus and operculo-parietal area 2 (OP2) – and their temporal metrics compared between groups. Partial Least Squares Correlation (PLSC) related CAPs to mood, vertigo, stress, and visual dependence for gait and postural control. Results Patients with PPPD showed altered dynamics seeded from rTPJ (decrease of a salience-coupled CAP, increased entries into a visual/dorsal-attention-coupled CAP), caudate nucleus (increased time in a default mode-coupled CAP, decrease of a salience/visual-coupled CAP) and hippocampus (increase of a default-mode-coupled CAP), but not OP2. PLSC yielded two significant latent components: the first linked rTPJ, OP2 and hippocampal CAPs sharing visual network co-deactivation to stress, mood, vertigo and visual dependence for gait; the second linked all caudate and two rTPJ CAPs to postural sway with eyes closed (visual dependence). Individual brain-behavior scores correlated in both groups. Conclusion Resting-state dynamics are altered in multisensory and motor regions in PPPD, but preserved in OP2, the core vestibular cortex. Brain-behavior organization appears shared across groups, with shifted dynamics in patients. Graphical abstract Curved arrows indicate dynamic functional connectivity patterns (Co-Activation Patterns) differing between patients with PPPD and HC (the direction is indicated by the small straight arrows). Dashed arrows indicate latent components of brain-behavior coupling identified through PLSC analysis. (rTPJ: right temporo-parietal junction; OP2: parietal operculum area 2; AP: antero-posterior).

item.title: Impact of hearing loss on visual selective attention: Evidence from N2pc and resting-state networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Efficient visual attention is fundamental to environmental adaptation and social interaction. While previous studies have observed alterations in visual processing among deaf individuals, findings remain controversial regarding whether these changes stem from hearing loss (sensory compensation vs. cognitive deficit) or sign language experience. To address this issue, the present study provides task-related and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) evidence to disentangle the specific drivers of visual selective attention plasticity. A visual search task was used to examine selective attention in 95 participants (34 prelingual deaf, 27 hearing signers, and 34 hearing nonsigners). Compared to both hearing groups, deaf individuals exhibited significantly lower hit rates and diminished N2-posterior contralateral (N2pc) amplitudes. Hearing signers and nonsigners showed comparable behavioral performance, N2pc amplitudes, and resting-state network topology, whereas the deaf group was further characterized by a degraded resting-state alpha network topology, evidenced by reduced clustering coefficients, global efficiency, and weakened frontal-occipital connectivity. N2pc amplitude correlated significantly with resting-state network properties and behavioral accuracy. These results suggest that deaf individuals may suffer from an imbalance in the regulation of visual selective attention, most clearly indexed by the evoked N2pc and by intrinsic alpha-network organization, and likely linked to increased resource competition following the loss of auditory monitoring. Our findings provide neurophysiological evidence that these attentional deficits are associated with hearing loss rather than with sign-language experience, offering a new perspective for understanding the boundaries of cross-modal plasticity in the human brain.

item.title: Prefrontal Cortical Changes With Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement in Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
JAMA psychiatry
Importance Despite decades of clinical implementation of medications for opioid use disorder (OUD), overdose mortality rates remain high, underscoring a critical need for interventions that target the brain mechanisms underlying addiction. Objective To assess the neural mechanisms of Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) and their associations with clinical outcomes, including craving and abstinence duration. Design, setting, and participants This randomized clinical trial was conducted from November 2020 to September 2024 among individuals with OUD recruited from an inpatient rehabilitation facility in New York and randomized to MORE or psychoeducational supportive therapy (PST). Data were analyzed from October 2024 to August 2026. Interventions Treatment with MORE (comprising training in mindfulness, drug cue reappraisal, and savoring positive experiences) or PST (active control condition) across 8 weekly 2-hour group sessions. Main outcomes and measures Outcomes included treatment-related changes in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) blood oxygen level-dependent signal (primary), abstinence length (secondary), and cue-induced craving (secondary). Results Drug cue reactivity task analyses included 59 participants (MORE, n = 24; 5 women [20.8%]; mean [SD] age, 43.6 [11.3] years; PST, n = 35; 8 women [22.9%]; mean [SD] age, 42.8 [10.0] years). Movie-watching and follow-up analyses were conducted in subsets of 37 (MORE, n = 18; PST, n = 19) and 38 participants (MORE, n = 13; PST, n = 25), respectively. Compared with PST, MORE reduced drug-biased activity in the middle frontal gyrus and other brain areas, including the precuneus, during downregulation of responses to drug cues relative to upregulation of responses to natural reward cues (even when controlling for passive cue viewing; z > 3.1; P < .05). The shift from drug to natural reward responses in the lateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (PFC) was associated with lower cue-induced craving exclusively in the MORE group (z > 3.1; P < .05). Relative to PST, MORE also reduced medial PFC synchronization to naturalistic drug-related movie scenes (q = 0.019) and significantly extended abstinence duration at follow-up (approximately 4 months posttreatment; χ2 = 6.7; P = .04; Cohen w = 0.19). Conclusions and relevance This neuroimaging randomized clinical trial demonstrates that MORE may restructure function in PFC nodes of the reward, salience, and control networks, positioning it as a biologically grounded adjunct to pharmacotherapy for OUD. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04112186.

item.title: Cerebello-basal ganglia networks and behavior across adulthood and aging
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The cerebellum contributes to aging, cognition, and reward related processing, but has been understudied in these domains. The cerebello-basal ganglia (CB-BG) circuit may be key to better understanding how the brain ages, as it has been implicated in modulation of cognitive, motor, and reward-related functions. Prior work has implicated this circuit in aging in a small sample, though it is also of interest in age-related neurodegenerative disease, particularly Parkinson’s Disease. Here, we investigated the CB-BG network in a sample of 138 participants between the ages of 35 and 86. Participants completed motor and cognitive testing batteries followed by 26 minutes of resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI), replicating previously mapped cognitive and motor subcircuits. When examining connectivity by age group (early and late middle age and older adulthood), we found higher functional connectivity in early middle age compared to older adulthood, with no results related to late middle age. Analysis of connectivity related to Stroop task performance showed higher connectivity-behavior associations in early middle-aged adults compared to older adults. Regarding sex differences, we found lower functional connectivity in females compared to males. Analysis of steroid hormone levels revealed higher connectivity associated with progesterone in females relative to males. We have replicated CB-BG subcircuits and further elucidated connectivity patterns associated with age, sex, progesterone levels, and cognitive performance. This expanded investigation of CB-BG networks represents an essential step in increasing our knowledge of age-related cognitive and motor declines and may be particularly relevant for consideration in Parkinson’s Disease.

item.title: Insula functional connectivity development follows a canonical antero-posterior axis of organization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The insula is a heterogeneous region associated with a range of functional domains including sensory, cognitive, and emotional processing. Cytoarchitectural and functional studies have described an antero-posterior axis of insula organization. However, the insula's functional development remains sparsely described. We delineated the development of insula resting-state functional connectivity across 562 individuals (6-22 years) using generalized additive models and population value decomposition. We show insulo-cortical functional connectivity development differs across the insula: anterior subregions have predominantly decreasing connectivity across the age range examined, whereas posterior subregions have variable connectivity that aligns with the sensorimotor-association axis. Vertex-level analysis revealed that age-related trajectories followed an antero-posterior axis that aligned with estimates of insula microstructure. Our results emphasize that the development of insula connectivity is spatially heterogeneous and aligns with known cytoarchitecture. The normative insula development described here provides a foundation for investigating how emerging psychopathology may be linked to variation in insula development.

item.title: Familiarity synchronizes brain rhythms during natural viewing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Our perception of the world is shaped not only by sensory information, but also by prior experience. However, how familiarity alters the coordination of neural representations across distributed brain networks remains unclear. Rhythmic neural activity provides a potential mechanism for coordinating information across sensory and higher-order brain regions in the light of previous experience. Here, we thus investigated whether familiarity alters the coordination of brain rhythms during naturalistic viewing. Participants who were either familiar or unfamiliar with the television series Game of Thrones viewed clips from the series while EEG or fMRI was recorded. We calculated the intersubject correlations of neural activity across EEG frequency bands and related this rhythmic activity to fMRI BOLD responses. Across participants, all brain rhythms showed reliable intersubject synchrony and related to activity across large-scale brain networks. Familiarity selectively enhanced intersubject synchronisation in beta and gamma rhythms, with these effects reflected in visual and default mode brain regions. Moreover, beta and gamma band activity were modulated by similar aspects of the movie, suggesting coordinated familiarity-related processing. These findings show that familiarity selectively shapes rhythmic neural dynamics across the cortex, providing a mechanism through which prior experience alters the coordination of neural representations during naturalistic perception.

item.title: Evaluating the mobile MUSE EEG headband for studying resting state EEG and event-related potentials
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
We examined whether and how tactile EEG experiments could be done through self-assessments by participants at home or through online experiments with consumer-grade mobile EEG devices. As a first step towards this aim, we performed a Flanker task in an online scenario with a MUSE headband and similarly a conventional lab experiment with a standard EEG device.Five undergraduate students participated in a visual flanker experiment and associated ERP components were recorded with either a standard 32-channel EEG System or a 4-channel MUSE EEG headband. In addition, we performed a 2-minutes resting state recording.Resting state brain oscillations measured with the Muse device revealed a similar pattern as with a standard EEG machine, however, strength of alpha oscillations was significantly reduced. For the Flanker task, in the Muse data, the stimulus-locked ERP components were less visible as compared to standard EEG, still the N200 was clearly expressed for the correct trials. Interestingly, in the incorrect trials, time-locked to the response there was the same negative Ne component visible as for the standard experiment. Our results reveal that the Muse device is suitable to obtain event-related potentials – even from interpolated electrode channels. Advanced preprocessing and artifact removal algorithms specifically targeting such devices with only a few and peripheral channels might help to better isolate ERP components of interest. It remains the challenge to develop devices and procedures for online tactile testing.

item.title: Neuroimaging Correlates of Adolescent Substance Use: A Systematic Review of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background: Neuroimaging may help characterize brain and contextual factors associated with substance use during development. The ABCD study supports investigation of developmental pathways relevant to substance use [1]. Objective: To synthesize original ABCD publications examining MRI measures in relation to substance use and substance-related exposures. Methods: The authors screened all 2,700 publications in the ABCD corpus. Original empirical articles reporting an MRI measure of any modality and a substance use variable were eligible; methodological, conceptual, review, and commentary articles were excluded. Imaging modality, brain measures, substances, design, and association direction were extracted for descriptive synthesis. Results: The evidence considered spans morphology, white matter microstructure, resting-state connectivity, and task activation. Findings concerning youth initiation, prenatal exposure, and familial liability address distinct developmental questions. Family history and stressful life events feature in the white matter literature [2]. Findings vary by modality, exposure definition, and temporal direction, and include null associations. Conclusions: The literature suggests distributed and context-dependent neuroimaging associations. Observational designs, overlapping participants, confounding, and analytic heterogeneity limit causal interpretation and assessment of independent replication. The findings support further longitudinal investigation but do not establish a validated MRI screening tool.

item.title: Impairment of mental time travel in patients with depressive disorders: Neural mechanisms and individual-level identification based on default mode network connectivity
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Mental time travel (MTT) enables re-experiencing past and pre-experiencing future events. Impairment in MTT is a core cognitive feature of major depressive disorder (MDD), but its neural mechanisms involving default mode network (DMN) functional connectivity remain unclear. Methods Thirty-six MDD patients and 36 healthy controls (HC) completed an adapted Autobiographical Memory Test to assess MTT. Resting-state fMRI examined DMN functional connectivity. Brain–behavior correlations used Spearman rank with Holm–Bonferroni correction. A support vector machine (SVM) classifier and support vector regression (SVR) evaluated individual discriminative and predictive values of identified connectivity features. Results Patients showed significantly reduced specificity in past recall and future imagination, with lower emotional valence, field perspective, and intensity. Resting-state connectivity revealed dissociated DMN patterns: weakened right anterior supramarginal gyrus–frontal pole, left frontal pole–posterior parietal, and hippocampus–lingual/cerebellar connections; enhanced left medial prefrontal–occipital and dorsal medial prefrontal–frontal pole connections. In HC, frontoparietal connectivity correlated with visual perspective; in patients, enhanced prefrontal connectivity negatively correlated with negative valence. Machine learning achieved 94.4% accuracy (AUC = 0.971) in classifying MDD vs HC, with frontal pole connections most discriminative. DMN connectivity significantly predicted individual specificity and neutral valence. Conclusions MTT impairment in MDD reflects system-level DMN imbalance and functional reorganization, providing neural targets for interventions. High individual classification accuracy supports DMN connectivity as a potential biomarker.

item.title: A generative framework for estimating brain energy landscapes from continuous neuroimaging observations.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Pairwise maximum entropy models (pMEMs) are gaining increasing attention as a principled way to study nonlinear brain-state transitions. By representing each brain region as a binary active/inactive state and estimating the least-biased probability distribution over all such network configurations, pMEMs reconstruct an energy landscape in which local minima correspond to stable or metastable brain states and transitions reflect movement across attractor basins. However, neuroimaging recordings are continuous and spatially mixed, forcing conventional pMEM analyses to demean and hard-threshold each channel. This ad hoc binarization discards amplitude information and can conflate spatially correlated noise or source mixing with genuine neural coupling. We introduce a hierarchical generative pMEM that links latent binary network states to continuous observations. Node-specific baseline and gain parameters model amplitude modulation, compound-symmetry noise captures shared residual covariance, and, for electroencephalography/magnetoencephalography (EEG/MEG), the electromagnetic leadfield is included as a generative forward model rather than a preprocessing inverse. Model parameters and latent states are jointly estimated using exact posterior enumeration for the small networks analyzed here and a mean-field extension for larger networks. Controlled simulations demonstrated two complementary advantages of the proposed framework. Residual-covariance modeling improved recovery of pMEM fields, couplings, and latent states by accounting for shared fluctuations, with the clearest gains when residual spatial correlation was sufficiently strong. The generative leadfield model further improved sensor-space inference by avoiding inverse-first source reconstruction, including settings in which covariance modeling alone offered limited gains. Resting-state EEG validation showed higher residual correlation during eyes-closed than eyes-open rest, consistent with elevated and spatially coherent alpha activity. Applied further to propofol sedation EEG (alpha-band amplitude envelopes, 8-13 Hz), the fitted 6-node default mode network (DMN) model showed pipeline-dependent condition effects in residual spatial correlation and basin entropy, not apparent under the conventional demean-based pMEM.

item.title: The path from brain to words is rerouted in opioid addiction
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Whether spontaneous speech preserves how the brain encoded an experience is unknown. We tested this question in opioid use disorder (OUD), in which drug cues outweigh other rewards. Eighty-two people with OUD and 34 controls watched the opening of the film Trainspotting during functional magnetic resonance imaging, then retold it in their own words. Language-model analyses showed that people with OUD dwelt on craving, personal identification and recovery, devoting more of their retelling to drug scenes. In 65 participants with imaging, this speech bias tracked how strongly the brain had distinguished drug from non-drug scenes during viewing, in left frontoparietal cortex in controls but left temporal cortex in OUD. Direct comparison showed left accumbens coupling positive in OUD and negative in controls, and left superior frontal coupling weaker in OUD. Spontaneous speech thus carries a trace of neural encoding whose route depends on what the experience meant to the speaker.

item.title: Beyond reduced alpha power: a weaker temporal link between alpha and other brain rhythms in Alzheimer’s disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background Reduced alpha power is among the most consistently reported resting electroencephalography (EEG) features of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, alpha activity also interacts with other rhythms over time, a dynamic aspect that power measures do not capture. Whether AD weakens this temporal interaction, and whether such a change carries information beyond reduced alpha power, remains unclear. Methods We analyzed public eyes-closed resting EEG from 29 healthy controls (HC), 36 patients with AD and 23 with frontotemporal dementia (FTD). After separating periodic from aperiodic activity, we tracked the aperiodic exponent and periodic theta, alpha, beta and gamma activity in consecutive 1-s windows. A vector autoregressive model predicted these five measures from the preceding window. Alpha’s predictive contribution ( G α ) was the increase in prediction error for theta, beta and gamma when the model was refitted without alpha as a predictor, with training and testing on separate time blocks of each recording. AD–HC differences were adjusted for age and sex, then for alpha expression (periodic alpha power) and signal quality (dynamic range and spatial reliability), with alpha self-persistence (alpha’s carry-over between windows) as a benchmark. We also tested whether expression and G α each added information about AD beyond the other. An exploratory Jansen–Rit-family circuit model examined whether expression and G α can change partly independently. Results G α was lower in AD than in HC (adjusted difference in 10³ G α , −3.19; 95% confidence interval −5.25 to −1.13; p = 0.0035), with a consistent direction across sensitivity analyses. Adjustment for alpha expression and signal quality retained 75.8% of this difference but only 4.4% of the self-persistence difference. Expression and G α each added information beyond the other (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012 for both). FTD contrasts were inconclusive. In the circuit model, reducing local recurrent excitation lowered alpha expression without an estimated decrease in G α , whereas reducing downstream input lowered G α with a smaller change in expression. Conclusions At the group level, the resting alpha abnormality in AD comprises two partly nonredundant dimensions: reduced expression and a weaker temporal link between alpha and subsequent multi-rhythm activity. Quantifying this temporal link may complement conventional spectral markers of AD.

item.title: From micro-architecture to networks: canonical neurobiological architecture of functional brain organization across the lifespan and in psychopathology
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Understanding how macroscale functional network connectivity (FNC) across the lifespan and in psychopathology is spatially organized with respect to microscale neurobiological architecture remains a challenge. Here, we constructed a cross-omics mapping framework by linking resting-state fMRI data (5,349 individuals, 6–80 years) with 49 neurobiological markers (24 cell types, 19 neurotransmitters, 6 mitochondria). We show that FNC development and aging unfold along cellular and molecular gradients. Specifically, spatial correspondence between age-related FNC changes and neurobiological microprofile networks varied by life stage, peaking for cell types in adolescence, neurotransmitter systems in mid-young adulthood and mitochondrial phenotypes in early adulthood. Applying normative modeling to 5 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), we identified disorder-specific and cross-disorder FNC phenotypes spatially associated with neurobiological architecture. Together, these findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking functional brain organization and dysfunction to canonical neurobiological architecture across the lifespan and psychiatric disorders.

item.title: Whole-brain normative modeling across multiple functional connectivity metrics in MEG
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Normative modeling has recently emerged in structural and functional neuroimaging as a promising approach to characterize neuropathology at the individual level. Trained on large healthy cohorts, these models predict expected measurements from covariates such as age and sex while quantifying normal population variability. Individual measurements can then be compared against the model to identify deviations associated with pathology. While most normative models of brain function have been based on functional MRI, EEG and MEG offer more direct measurements of brain activity at higher temporal resolution. Despite the promise, how to adequately perform normative modelling at the whole-brain level on these modalities remains challenging. We here propose M/EEG-FUNCOIN to identify age- and sex-related dimensions of change in functional connectivity from a plethora of FC measures from electrophysiology: amplitude envelope correlation, phase-locking value, and time-delay embedding covariance. Using resting-state MEG data from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset, we show that M/EEG-FUNCOIN can: (i) characterize age- and sex-related whole-brain functional connectivity patterns in greater detail than existing methods; and (ii) effectively capture meaningful deviations in connectivity in individuals that rank high and low in cognitive ability. Altogether, these results show great potential for applications in complex, network-level brain pathology.

item.title: Functional and Structural Brain Age Gaps as Complementary Predictive Markers for Cognitive Performance
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cognitive decline is characterized by substantial inter-individual variability across the lifespan, even among clinically healthy adults. However, it is unclear how structural and functional brain organization jointly relate to differences in cognitive performance within the typical populations. We considered a multimodal brain age framework by predicting for each subject its age from either structural MRI or resting-state functional MRI, after training on the 1000BRAINS cohort (901 participants, 18-85 years). Following, a structural and a functional brain age gap markers were defined as the deviations with respect to the real chronological age. We then used the markers to characterize the interplay between structure and function in shaping cognitive performances. Our findings reveal that the functional marker is as important to predict global cognitive performance as the structural marker. The most accurate prediction was found for global cognition, executive functions and episodic memory, followed by working memory, attention and language. In particular, the structural marker was contributing to all domains, except for working memory, whereas the functional marker had the highest contribution. Overall, structural and functional brain age models together provide a meaningful subject-level summary of brain information for predicting cognition, supporting a multidimensional view of typical aging.

item.title: Resting-state alpha scale-free dynamics predict individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values during free choice
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Values learned through reward can continue to influence choices guided by one's own preferences, such as which painting to hang, to an extent that varies across individuals. Because such preferences build up gradually across choices, their expression may depend on how well internally generated states are sustained over time, a property indexed by long-range temporal correlations (LRTC) in intrinsic brain activity. We tested whether resting-state alpha-band LRTC predicts individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values. Eighty-one participants learned through probabilistic feedback which of four abstract shapes tended to be rewarded, and then judged their preferences among these shapes and 11 new shapes without feedback. Alpha LRTC was estimated by detrended fluctuation analysis of resting-state electroencephalography recorded before, between, and after the tasks. A trial-level mixed-effects model showed that reward history influenced preference judgments and that this influence decreased with resting-state alpha LRTC: participants with weak LRTC chose high-reward shapes over new shapes on 75% of trials, whereas those with strong LRTC were close to indifference (54%). The relationship was distributed across the scalp, stable across recordings, and not explained by spectral power or learning performance. Resting-state alpha LRTC is thus related to how strongly reward-learned values are carried into preference-based choice. Given the view that stronger LRTC reflects a longer window over which internally generated states are integrated, the observed relationship could arise because the window is biased toward values built up through one's own choices, or because it attenuates values learned under a criterion that no longer applies; which account holds remains to be determined.
